In Durban, Zanele heard her mother on the phone in the kitchen. "Sorry, I'm stuck in traffic, I'll be there in twenty minutes." Layla was standing at the stove in her slippers.
Zanele frowned. Last week she had been sent to her room for saying she had fed the dog when she hadn't.
Layla hung up and saw her daughter's face. She was quiet for a moment. Then she called her friend back. "Actually, I'm still at home. I lost track of time. I'm sorry. I'll leave in five."
She turned to Zanele. "That was a lie, and I didn't like hearing myself say it. I'm working on it too." Zanele's shoulders dropped. That night, without being asked, she admitted she hadn't brushed her teeth.

qa.q: What did Layla first say on the phone?
qa.a: "Sorry, I'm stuck in traffic, I'll be there in twenty minutes."

qa.q: What might Zanele have been thinking when she frowned?
qa.a: She was probably thinking it was unfair, since she had been sent to her room last week for the same kind of small lie.

qa.q: Which choice by Layla taught honesty best?
qa.a: She called back to correct the lie and openly told Zanele it was a lie she was working on, showing that adults own their errors.

qa.q: What did Layla's honesty mean for Zanele, and what shows it?
qa.a: It made honesty feel fair and shared; Zanele's shoulders dropped and she admitted not brushing her teeth without being asked.

grounding: A girl catches her mother in a small phone lie, and the mother's open correction teaches more about honesty than any lecture.

passage:
In Class 5, Farida Ma'am was drawing a map on the board. "The Arctic is the biggest ocean," she said. Sarika's hand went up slowly. "Ma'am, I think the book says the Pacific."
Some children held their breath. Last year's teacher used to get angry when corrected.
Farida Ma'am opened the textbook, read, and laughed a little. "You're right. I was wrong. Thank you, Sarika." She crossed out the word and wrote PACIFIC in big letters. "Fix your notes, everyone. I get things wrong too."
After the bell Sarika stayed behind, twisting her bag strap. "Ma'am, in Friday's test I looked at someone's answer for question four." Farida Ma'am nodded. "Thank you for telling me. We'll redo it together tomorrow."

qa.q: What did Farida Ma'am write on the board after checking?
qa.a: She crossed out the word and wrote PACIFIC in big letters.

qa.q: Why were some children holding their breath?
qa.a: They were nervous because last year's teacher got angry when corrected, so they expected trouble for Sarika.

qa.q: What did Farida Ma'am show by admitting her mistake?
qa.a: She showed that adults get things wrong too and can own it openly, which made honesty feel safe in class.

qa.q: How did Farida Ma'am's example affect Sarika?
qa.a: It made Sarika feel safe enough to stay behind and admit looking at someone's answer in Friday's test.

grounding: A teacher owns her mistake openly in front of the class, and her example makes a pupil brave enough to confess a mistake too.

passage:
I live next door to Rafiq and his son Chetan, and the walls are thin.
On Tuesday evening Rafiq's phone rang. I heard him say, "Tell them I'm not home," and Chetan, who is about nine, answered and said, "Abbu isn't home." Then a small pause. "Abbu, you are home."
Later I saw them on the balcony. I couldn't hear all of it, and I don't know what Rafiq was thinking. But I heard him say, "You're right. I made you lie for me. That was wrong." Chetan asked why he did it. Rafiq said, "I didn't want to talk to my boss. That's not a good reason."
The next morning I heard Rafiq on the phone again, loud enough through the wall: "Sir, yesterday I asked my son to say I wasn't home. I was. I'm sorry." Chetan was standing right beside him.

qa.q: What did Rafiq ask Chetan to say on the phone?
qa.a: Tell them I'm not home.

qa.q: How did Rafiq seem to feel on the balcony?
qa.a: Rafiq seemed ashamed and regretful, admitting he had made his son lie for him and that his reason was not good.

qa.q: What did Rafiq do that teaches honesty better than a lecture?
qa.a: He openly owned his error to Chetan and then called his boss to admit the truth while Chetan stood beside him.

qa.q: How might Chetan see his father's phone call the next morning?
qa.a: Chetan probably feels proud and learns that adults fix their mistakes too, not just children.

grounding: A neighbour observes a father who made his son tell a white lie on the phone owning the error openly, modelling honesty.

passage:
Friday. On the city bus, the conductor asked Shankar's age. His mother Vasudha said, "Five," though he was seven, to avoid buying his ticket. Shankar stared at her.
Sunday. At the fair, the ticket counter asked Shankar's age for the ride. "Five," he said confidently. Vasudha went red. "He's seven," she told the attendant, and paid.
Later, on the walk home, Shankar asked, "Why was it wrong for me? You said five on the bus."
Vasudha stopped under a streetlight. Her cheeks burned. "You're right. I did it first. It was wrong when I did it too." She took his hand.
Tuesday. On the bus again, the conductor asked. Before Shankar could speak, Vasudha said, "He's seven. One full, one child," and counted out the coins. She glanced at Shankar. He smiled, a little surprised, and sat up very straight.

qa.q: How old was Shankar really?
qa.a: He was seven.

qa.q: How did Vasudha feel when Shankar asked why it was wrong for him?
qa.a: Vasudha felt ashamed and embarrassed, her cheeks burning, because she saw he had copied her own dishonesty.

qa.q: What did Vasudha do that taught honesty best?
qa.a: She admitted to Shankar that she did it first and it was wrong, then showed it by paying the correct fare on Tuesday.

qa.q: How does Shankar react when his mother tells the truth on Tuesday?
qa.a: Shankar feels surprised and proud, smiling and sitting up very straight.

grounding: It shows a child copying his mother's small dishonesty and the mother owning her error openly, teaching more than a lecture.

passage:
Lavanya, you caught me cheating at ludo just now, and I laughed it off. Sit. Your Charu Nani owes you a story, and an apology.
When your Mama was about eight, I used to play carrom with him every evening. And I cheated. Small things, moving the striker a little, pretending not to see my own foul.
One day his teacher sent a note home: he had been caught moving his counters in a class game. I scolded him. "Where did you learn such a thing?"
He looked at me and said, "From you, Amma."
I sat down on the floor. There was nothing to say. Then I told him, "You're right. I cheated, and I'm sorry. From today, we both play fair."
So, Lavanya. I moved my piece. That was wrong. Shall we start again?

qa.q: What did young Charu's son say when she asked where he learned to cheat?
qa.a: He said, "From you, Amma."

qa.q: How did young Charu feel when her son answered?
qa.a: Charu felt ashamed and stunned, sitting down on the floor with nothing to say.

qa.q: What choice in the story taught the son about honesty?
qa.a: Charu admitted she had cheated, apologised, and promised they would both play fair from that day.

qa.q: How might Lavanya feel when Nani admits cheating at ludo?
qa.a: Lavanya would likely feel surprised and respected, seeing an adult own a mistake instead of laughing it off.

grounding: A grandmother tells how her small cheating was copied by her son and how owning the error openly taught more than a lecture.

The rain was pouring, the car was stuck in traffic, and Vikas was already late to pick up his sister from the station. His phone rang. It was his boss.
"Sorry, sir, I'm in a meeting, I'll call back," he said, and hung up.
From the back seat, nine-year-old Amandeep said, "Papa, you're not in a meeting. You're in the car."
Vikas opened his mouth to say, "That's different, grown-ups have to." Then he closed it.
"You're right," he said. "I told a lie because I didn't want to talk right now. That was lazy of me."
He called his boss back. "Sir, sorry, I wasn't in a meeting. I'm driving in the rain. Can I call you in half an hour?" The boss said that was fine.
Amandeep grinned. "You got caught."
"I did," Vikas said. "And I'm glad it was by you."

qa.q: What did Vikas tell his boss the first time?
qa.a: 'Sorry, sir, I'm in a meeting, I'll call back.'

qa.q: How did Amandeep feel when Papa owned the lie?
qa.a: Amandeep was amused and pleased, grinning 'You got caught', seeing Papa admit it instead of making excuses.

qa.q: What did Vikas do that taught more than a lecture?
qa.a: He admitted the lie in front of Amandeep, called his boss back with the truth, and didn't hide behind 'grown-ups have to'.

qa.q: How might Vikas feel being corrected by his child?
qa.a: Vikas was briefly tempted to defend it, but seemed glad and a little humbled to be caught by Amandeep.

grounding: Shows a father caught by his child in a phone white lie owning it openly, teaching honesty better than any lecture.
